 Posted November 19, 2026 at 8:00 am by Celine McNicholas , Samantha Sanders , and Ben Zipperer 
 The new Congress can’t tackle affordability without raising the minimum wage 
 Affordability—or the lack thereof—has dominated the political debate in the U.S. and was the driving concern for voters in the midterm election. And for good reason. Across the country, too many families are struggling to make ends meet, and their message at the ballot box was clear. They want change, and they expect their elected representatives to deliver it. As the new Congress considers an affordability agenda to help working families, lawmakers must understand that a key reason paychecks no longer stretch to cover the essentials is suppressed pay—not prices alone. 
 For decades, policymakers have neglected reforms that would strengthen workers’ bargaining power and raise wages, fueling a growing gap between productivity and typical workers’ pay. Had their pay kept pace with productivity over the past 45 years, it would be roughly 40% higher today. So if Congress wants to address affordability, it must pass legislation that raises workers’ wages. This includes labor law reform that ensures workers have a real right to a union and collective bargaining, which helps them win higher pay and better benefits. It also includes raising the federal minimum wage, which is one of the most direct levers Congress has to put more money in workers’ pockets.
 Next year will mark 20 years since Congress last raised the federal minimum wage. Currently standing at $7.25 per hour, its lowest real value in 77 years, the outdated federal minimum wage is a major driver of the affordability crisis facing low-wage workers. In the absence of federal action, many states have raised the minimum wage for their residents. Thanks in large part to the Fight for $15 campaign, 21 states and the District of Columbia —home to half of all U.S. wage earners—will have a minimum wage of at least $15 by 2028. But that patchwork still leaves about 55 million workers who live in 20 states with a $7.25 minimum wage.
 Earlier this year, EPI released a report calling on Congress to raise the federal minimum wage to two-thirds of the national median wage—equivalent to roughly $17.50 today, and a projected $20 in 2030. Our proposed benchmark would lift pay for nearly 40 million workers, about a quarter of the workforce. It would also eliminate poverty wages and move the federal floor toward a living wage in much of the country, so that a single adult working full time could cover modest expenses in half of U.S. counties, according to EPI’s Family Budget Calculator thresholds.
 Raising the minimum wage is the single quickest policy to improve affordability for the greatest number of workers. Time and time again, minimum wage increases have raised wages with little-to-no effect on the number of jobs. The income increases they generate are transformative for low-income families and far outweigh the small effects they have on prices. Indexing the minimum wage so it adjusts each year to stay at two-thirds of the median wage would lock in those gains and also durably narrow the gap between low-wage workers and the typical worker, with Black workers and women seeing the largest benefits. Congress could raise the federal minimum wage to $17.50 in a single increase effective tomorrow with no job loss concerns. Several proposals in the 119th Congress would raise the federal minimum wage. They include target minimum wages ranging from $15 to as high as $25, phase-in schedules running from 2026 to 2038, and different forms of indexing minimum wages to keep pace with either inflation or wages.
 Table 1 below provides further information on these bills, including the number of congressional cosponsors on each measure as of November 16. These proposals lay the groundwork for action on the minimum wage in the incoming Congress.
 The 120th Congress has the chance to advance a true affordability agenda that raises wages for U.S. workers. A core element of that agenda must be raising the federal minimum wage. This should be achievable, considering that more than a third of the newly elected members of Congress called for raising the minimum wage in their campaign platforms. Table 2 below lists those members and their state minimum wages. Thanks to workers and advocates who have fought for and won state and local wage increases, the new Congress can consider a bold federal minimum wage increase. And it can afford to be bold, since research shows that Congress could more than double the federal minimum wage—raising it to $17.50 tomorrow with no significant job loss impacts. Congress must also index the federal minimum wage to median wage growth to keep the floor from losing ground to inflation or falling behind the broader economy. That will ensure that U.S. workers are never again left for decades with no increase in the federal minimum wage.
